doc.title: Larry Ridley interviewed by Monk Rowe, Toronto, Canada, January 10, 2003

chapter: Jazz in the academy and critics
title: Critics who skip homework, and Leonard Feather on the origin of jazz polls
summary: Critics should study and consult musicians; Leonard Feather explained how the magazine polls began, and Ridley calls them political.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Critics, polls and the jazz press

blocks.x: mission and I have no problem with him, that’s what he does, it’s music that you can talk over, have in the background. It’s not like when I hear Charlie Parker and I stop and say oh wow, check that out what he did going through that chord change. You know Kenny’s found his niche and hey, God bless him. He’s doing his thing. But it’s just very interesting when people in situations like this take it upon themselves to make these wild assumptions and to misinform people. And we need to do away with that kind of stuff. And if he doesn’t know the answer to a certain kind of thing he doesn’t have to fabricate anything. And that’s what a lot of people do. It’s the problem with a lot of writers and a lot of critics. They don’t do their homework, they don’t check with musicians, they don’t understand the musician’s point of view. They don’t take the time to understand. They don’t study the history of the music because it’s still just their opinion. But many of them are in certain positions where they can make or break, just like the theater critics do with plays that are on Broadway or other things. They make or break peoples’ careers with what they say. But I think that all of these people who put themselves in that position and sort of posture themselves as being authorities or experts need to make sure that they have really, really done their homework. Otherwise I don’t want to talk to them. I really don’t. And the whole thing about jazz polls. I had a long conversation with Leonard Feather. Leonard Feather told me that the jazz polls started because as a young man coming here to the United States he was totally enamored with jazz. And he expected when he came to the states that he was going to find these jazz musicians wearing nothing but the finest clothes, riding around in limousines and having these fantastic women on their arm and living in mansions and blah, blah, blah. He had this whole fantasy going. When he gets here he finds out a lot of these musicians were just struggling and starving. So he went to the magazines and started pitching them — why aren’t you talking about these great musicians that you have here? And they told him point blank he said, we are only interested in selling magazines. If you can come up with an idea that will help us to sell magazines we’ll be glad to incorporate that. So that’s when he came up with the Esquire and Metronome and the Down Beat polls and that’s how that became a factor in the jazz community. And it’s kind of gotten out of hand because it’s become very political, I mean a lot of people don’t know but the ballot boxes are stuffed. It’s almost like the Florida election.

Where we finally, or for the first time, had a president elected by the Supreme Court as opposed to the President appointing the Supreme Court. But that’s another story, right Monk? But some of the same elements. Like people stuffing the ballot box, and industry buying time and promoting their artists and this, that and the other, so it becomes incumbent upon them — the Grammys — we know that that’s all political.
